To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the left hemisphere is more involved in lexical processing than the right hemisphere.

the RVF advantage for word processing is not reduced by the proportion of imageable words in a list and that the RVF LH advantage for word processing increases as the proportion of nonimageable words in a word list increases.
the RVF advantage for word recognition was unaltered for high image words, but increased as the proportion low image words increased.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of hemispheric specialization in language processing, and more particularly the role of hemifield specialization in word recognition.
the role of imagery in word recognition.
the question of how the brain processes information.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the RVF is specialized for the processing of high-image nouns, and that the LH is specialized for the recognition of low-image nouns.

there is no clear evidence for a right hemisphere advantage for the processing of words with a high imagery content, and that the right hemisphere is more involved in the processing of low-imagery than high-imagery words.
the RVF advantage for words is reduced when the proportion of low-imagery nouns in the list increases.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the left hemisphere (LVF/LH) advantage for high imageable words is not influenced by the proportion of imageable words presented in the stimulus list.
there is a significant RVF advantage for word recognition.
the RVF-LH advantage for word processing is a function of word class and word class proportion.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the word-class effect is not a function of the proportion of imageable and nonimageable words presented in a lexical decision task.
the RVF advantage for word recognition does not vary as a function of word imageability when word-class proportions are varied.
the proportion of high/low-image words in the list context affects the RVF/LHF advantage.
